---
title: "How to Turn Your Work Files into an AI Knowledge Base with Microsoft 365 Copilot"
subtitle: "A practical 6-step setup so your team can ask plain-English questions and get answers from your own documents"
category: "how-to"
audience: "business"
read_time_minutes: 7
tags: ["microsoft-365", "copilot", "sharepoint", "data-organisation", "business-ai"]
---

> **In short:** Microsoft 365 Copilot can read the Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files you already store in SharePoint and answer questions about them in plain English. It needs a paid Copilot licence (around $30 USD per user per month, roughly $45 AUD), admin access to switch it on, and your documents sitting in SharePoint rather than scattered across personal drives. Below are the real steps to get there.

A new starter joins on Monday and needs the refund policy by lunch. Instead of pinging three people and digging through shared drives, they type one question into Copilot and get a sourced answer in seconds. That is what a working AI knowledge base looks like. Here is how to build one without writing code.

## Before you start

You need four things in place before Step 1:

- **A Microsoft 365 Business subscription** (Basic, Standard or Premium). Personal Microsoft accounts do not support this setup.
- **A Microsoft 365 Copilot licence for each user** — a paid add-on, around **$30 USD per user per month** (about $45 AUD) as of 2026. Confirm the current price on Microsoft's pricing page, as it can shift.
- **Admin access** to the Microsoft 365 admin centre, or an IT person who can help with the setup step below.
- **Your files already saved in SharePoint Online**, not just sitting on personal OneDrives or local laptops.

You will also need a **modern browser** (Edge or Chrome) and a **Teams or Outlook account** so you can talk to Copilot at the end.

## Step 1 — Move your documents into a SharePoint document library

Open your team's SharePoint site in the browser and pick (or create) the document library where your work files should live. Click the **"New"** button at the top of the library, then **"File upload"** or **"Folder upload"** to drag in your existing PDFs, Word documents, Excel sheets and PowerPoint decks.

You will see your uploaded files appear in the library list with thumbnails and the date they were added. **You'll know it worked when** the files show up in the library view and you can click one to open it in the browser.

💬 *Tip: name your folders by topic, not by date — "Client Onboarding" beats "2024 Stuff".*

## Step 2 — Check the file formats Copilot can actually read

Copilot works best with **Word (.docx), Excel (.xlsx), PowerPoint (.pptx), PDF and plain text files** that already contain selectable text. Scanned PDFs that look like photos will not be searchable until you run them through OCR (text recognition — software that reads the image and turns it back into editable text).

Open a few of your key documents and try to highlight the text inside. If you can copy and paste words from the PDF, it is ready. If you cannot, it needs OCR first.

**You'll know it worked when** you can select and copy text out of every important document without it coming out as garbage characters.

## Step 3 — Review who can see what

Copilot only shows people documents they already have permission to open. If a folder is wide open to the whole company, Copilot will happily share that information with anyone who asks. This is the most important step to get right.

In your document library, click the **"Settings"** icon (the gear) at the top right, then look for **"Library settings"** or **"Permissions"**. Review which groups have access. For sensitive folders — payroll, client contracts, HR — restrict access to just the people who need it.

**You'll know it worked when** a test user from outside the right group gets an "Access denied" message when they try to open the folder.

💬 *Tip: ask your IT admin to create security groups like "Marketing Team" and "Finance Team" so you can assign folder access by team, not by individual name.*

## Step 4 — Switch on Copilot in the admin centre

This is where your IT admin comes in. They need to log into the **Microsoft 365 admin centre** and assign the Copilot licence to each user who should have it. The exact menu path can shift as Microsoft updates the interface, but it generally sits under **Billing or Licences**. Search for "Microsoft 365 Copilot" and assign licences to the right people.

After a few minutes, those users will see a Copilot icon appear in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams. It can take up to 24 hours for licences to fully activate across the system.

**You'll know it worked when** a licensed user opens Word and sees the Copilot panel on the right-hand side of the screen.

## Step 5 — Ask Copilot your first real question

Open Copilot from the side panel in Teams, or in Word, and type a question the way you would ask a colleague: *"What does our refund policy say about digital products?"* or *"Summarise last quarter's sales report from the Marketing library."*

Copilot will search your permitted SharePoint files and return a written answer with **citations** — clickable links back to the exact document and section it used. If the answer is wrong, the right file is usually missing, badly named, or in a folder you cannot access.

**You'll know it worked when** you get a confident, sourced answer (not a "I cannot find that" response) and clicking the citation opens the right document.

💬 *Example prompt to copy:* *"Based on the policy documents in our HR library, summarise the parental leave entitlements for full-time staff."*

## Step 6 — Tidy up based on what you learn

After a week of use, ask your team which questions Copilot answered well and which it fumbled. The fumbled ones usually point to missing files, confusing file names, or permissions that block the AI.

Spend 30 minutes renaming the worst offenders, moving strays into the right libraries, and tightening permissions on sensitive folders. This small cleanup is what separates a Copilot setup your team trusts from one they quietly stop using.

**You'll know it worked when** your team starts using Copilot unprompted for everyday questions instead of emailing you for documents.

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake:** Assuming Copilot can read scanned PDFs. **Fix:** Run them through OCR first using OneDrive's built-in OCR, Adobe Acrobat, or your scanner's "searchable PDF" option.
- **Mistake:** Leaving sensitive folders open to everyone in SharePoint. **Fix:** Use SharePoint's permission settings to restrict access by group, and audit access before turning Copilot on.
- **Mistake:** Uploading files with names like "Document1 FINAL v3 (2).docx". **Fix:** Rename files with descriptive, searchable names like "Client-Acme-Proposal-2026.docx" so Copilot and your team can both find them.
- **Mistake:** Expecting Copilot to invent answers when the document is missing. **Fix:** If Copilot says it cannot find something, the file is probably not in SharePoint yet — check OneDrive and local drives for strays.

## What this means for you

- **If you run a small business:** This setup is realistic once you have 10 or more users with admin support. For one or two people, a simpler tool like Google NotebookLM lets you upload files and ask questions without any admin work.
- **If you manage a team:** The biggest payoff is onboarding — new starters ask Copilot instead of interrupting colleagues. Plan a 30-minute cleanup of your SharePoint folders before you switch it on.
- **If you are worried about privacy:** Copilot respects your existing SharePoint permissions. If a document is locked down, Copilot will not share it with someone who should not see it. Start with a non-sensitive library to build trust before rolling out company-wide.
